items.verified_answer: Yes, $x(x+1)$ and $x^2+x$ are equal for every real $x$. Reason: by the distributive law of multiplication over addition in the real number system ($a(b+c) = ab + ac$), multiplying $x$ across $(x+1)$ yields $x \cdot x + x \cdot 1 = x^2 + x$. Because this equality is derived from the fundamental field axioms of real arithmetic and laws of exponents, it constitutes an algebraic identity holding for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, not merely an empirical coincidence at tested values.

items.verified_answer: The constructed linear polynomial is $p(x) = -2x + 2$. Verification: (1) Constant term is $p(0) = -2(0) + 2 = 2$; (2) Zero is $p(1) = -2(1) + 2 = 0$; (3) Degree is 1 ($a = -2 \ne 0$). Exactly one linear polynomial satisfies these conditions: any linear polynomial has form $ax+b$ ($a \ne 0$); condition $p(0)=2$ forces $b=2$, and condition $p(1)=0$ forces $a(1)+2=0 \implies a=-2$. Since the linear system for coefficients has a unique solution, no other linear polynomial can satisfy them.
